Chapter 9—Finding New Purpose: Redefining Success and Identity
You know, after spending years chasing someone else's idea of success, there's this moment—a quiet one, sometimes unsettling—where you ask yourself, "What now?" All those old signposts—the status in the church, getting approval from leaders, the applause—suddenly, they just don't mean what they used to.
So, how do you start measuring a good life when the old rulebook doesn't apply anymore? At first, searching for a new purpose can feel like standing in front of a blank canvas. Some days, nothing clicks. The future feels wide open, but also a little bit intimidating.
But here's the beautiful thing—step by step, new passions begin to show up. Maybe it's speaking up for others, telling your own story, or lending a hand to someone who's stumbling through their own struggles. Suddenly, these moments start to fill the emptiness with something real—something meaningful.
Picture this: you meet a young person, right when they're wrestling with their own crisis of faith. The conversation is unfiltered, maybe even messy, but there's honesty in it. As you offer support, you realize—your own pain, those old wounds—they can actually help someone else. What used to feel like a mark of shame now feels more like a badge of survival.
Even work starts to look different. Projects that once felt pointless suddenly matter. There's this quiet sense of responsibility—like, maybe you've got a platform, a voice, and some hard-earned experience that could make things better for others. And that old fear of being seen as a troublemaker? It just kind of fades away, replaced by a gentle confidence that comes from living your truth.
Most people spend their whole lives searching for purpose. But when you've lost everything you thought you needed, that search becomes even more urgent—and, honestly, more rewarding. Because now, you get to decide what success means. On your own terms. And really, that's the greatest gift of all.
